title: Inflation Hits 3.8%, Highest in Three Years, as Americans’ Spending Power Erodes
summary: Inflation accelerated in April to its highest level in three years, squeezing household budgets and creating political headwinds for President Trump and congressional Republicans with midterm elections just five months away. The Commerce Department reported Thursday that the personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.5% in March. On a monthly basis, prices increased 0.4%, a slowdown from March’s 0.7% jump but still above the Federal Reserve’s comfort zone. The report showed broad-based price increases: gasoline, groceries, clothing, and electricity all climbed. Services like dental visits, car repairs, and vet bills also spiked. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy, rose 0.3% monthly, signaling that underlying price pressures are building. Meanwhile, Americans’ inflation-adjusted after-tax incomes fell for the third consecutive month, and real consumer spending barely rose. “Signs of stress are building inside the American household,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. The data complicates the Fed’s path. With inflation well above the 2% target, policymakers may forego rate cuts this year; some officials have hinted the next move could be a rate hike under new Chair Kevin Warsh. Higher borrowing costs would further strain consumers. Yet Trump and some aides have downplayed the pain. Trump called the 50% surge in gas prices since the Iran war began “peanuts,” and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent revived the term “transitory” to describe inflation—a word that backfired during the 2021-22 spike. Economists are skeptical. Dan North of Allianz Trade noted that multiple inflation pressures, including tariffs and AI-driven demand for tech equipment, are in the pipeline. The economy grew at a modest 1.6% annual rate in the first quarter, but consumer spending growth slowed to 1.4%. With gas averaging $4.43 a gallon and prices still climbing, voters’ economic anxieties could shape the November elections.
why_it_matters: Rising inflation means that families have less money for necessities and extras, and it may lead to higher interest rates for anyone with a car loan or college savings plan. The frustration could also shift political winds, determining which leaders and policies will shape their future.

background_read: The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index is the Federal Reserve’s preferred way of measuring inflation because it captures a wide range of goods and services. Core inflation strips out food and energy to reveal underlying trends. A rate of 3.8% is far above the Fed’s 2% target, and the last time inflation stayed this elevated for a sustained period was in 2022 after pandemic-related supply chain disruptions and government stimulus.

President Donald Trump took office again in 2025. His administration has imposed new tariffs on imported goods, which can raise prices for consumers. The new Fed Chair, Kevin Warsh, faces the difficult choice of keeping rates high to fight inflation, which could slow the economy and raise unemployment.

During 2021-22, officials repeatedly called inflation 'transitory,' but it proved to be stubborn, damaging their credibility. Now Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s use of the same word is drawing skepticism from economists, who point to ongoing cost pressures from tariffs and strong demand for technology equipment driven by artificial intelligence. With midterm elections approaching, a dissatisfied electorate could punish the party in power.

perspectives.description: Some economists and administration officials argue that inflation partly reflects a still-growing economy with strong consumer demand and heavy investment in technology. They suggest that as supply chains adjust, inflation may ease on its own without drastic Fed action.

Critics highlight that inflation is outpacing wage gains, causing real incomes to fall and forcing families to cut back even on basics. They note that trade tariffs and dismissive comments like 'peanuts' downplay real financial suffering and risk making voters feel ignored.

The data reveals that inflation is broad-based and not just a temporary spike; core inflation shows sticky price increases. Tariffs and AI-driven demand for equipment create supply-side cost pressures, meaning the Federal Reserve may have limited room to lower rates without reigniting inflation.

If the Fed is forced to raise rates, borrowing costs for mortgages, businesses, and student loans will climb, potentially slowing the economy further. Voter anxiety over high prices could lead to significant political changes in the upcoming midterms, altering the direction of economic policy.
